subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If Q(h,k) is the foot of the perpendicular of P(x₁,y₁) on the line ax+by+c=0 then prove that (h−x₁) : a = (k−y₁) : b = −(ax₁+by₁+c) : (a²+b²).

mark_split.label: Write h and k through r

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.18 — LAQ chapter 1 The Straight Line, answer 5.1. Printed appearance: AP 20. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this LAQ chapter. It is not a bare guess: the book prints its own numbered 'Step-1 / Step-2 / Step-3' structure against this very answer, and the split follows those printed steps, giving the two long eliminations two marks each and the closing solve two, with one for setting up. The only printed splits in this UNIT are on SAQ answer 59 (book p.63, 1+1+2) and VSAQ answer 98 (p.83, 1+1) — both shorter cuts, so neither fixes a 7-mark shape. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. ⚠ The book prints a note between answers 5.1 and 5.2 reading 'First half of the solution is same to same' — the two proofs share their first three steps EXACTLY, and differ only in the closing condition. The step ids and labels here are deliberately identical across the two files for that reason, which follows the Maths-1A precedent of giving one method over different conditions one shared skeleton. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. NOTE: The Straight Line is the FIRST Maths-1B unit to occupy ALL THREE sections of the paper — the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.3) gives it 2+2 marks in Section A, 4 in Section B and 7 in Section C, 15 in all, tying Differentiation as the highest-scoring unit on the paper. It therefore has three separate chapters in this book: LAQ chapter 1 (book pp.14-18), SAQ chapter 9 (pp.61-64) and VSAQ chapter 14 (pp.79-82). All three boundaries were walked: p.19 opens Pair of Straight Lines, p.65 opens Limits & Continuity, and p.83 opens 3-D Coordinates. The book's separate STAR QUESTIONS PLUS bank (pp.104-108) contributes three more, answers 182-184, authored here as sqp1-sqp3. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Find r from the condition.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what perpendicularity gives you, and what condition on Q finishes it.

steps.label: Both slopes
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two slopes are needed — the one joining the two points, and the one of the given line. The second reads straight off the coefficients as −a/b.
steps.memory_tip: Two slopes: the one joining P and Q, and the line's own, which reads off as −a/b.
lines: Slope of PQ is  m₁ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (k − y₁)/(h − x₁)
Slope of the line ax + by + c = 0 is  m₂ = −a/b

recall.must_convey: That the slope of PQ is (k − y₁)/(h − x₁) and the slope of the line is −a/b.
accept: slope of P Q is k minus y one over h minus x one and the line's slope is minus a over b
write both slopes, one from the two points and one from the coefficients
the line a x plus b y plus c has slope minus a over b
rendu slopes rayali, P Q di and line di
both slopes first

steps.why: Everything in this proof follows from PQ being perpendicular to the line, so both slopes have to be on the page before that fact can be used.
common_mistakes: Writing the slope of PQ upside down.

steps.label: Draw P, the line and the foot
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. The picture carries the one fact the second half turns on: Q sits ON the line, so its coordinates satisfy the line's equation.
steps.memory_tip: The picture carries the fact the second half turns on: Q sits ON the line.

recall.must_convey: That P, the line and the foot Q are sketched, with Q lying on the line. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw P above the line and drop a perpendicular to Q on the line
sketch the point, the line and the foot of the perpendicular
show Q lying on the line with a right angle at Q
P nunchi perpendicular geesi Q ni line meeda mark cheyyali
draw the foot of the perpendicular

steps.why: The foot of a perpendicular lies ON the line by definition — the drawing is what makes that obvious, and it is the only thing separating this proof from its neighbour.
common_mistakes: Drawing Q off the line, which is the image rather than the foot.
Omitting the right-angle mark, which is the whole reason PQ is perpendicular.

steps.label: Use the perpendicularity
steps.margin_note: Two marks. PQ meets the line at a right angle, so m₁m₂ = −1. Rearranged, that says (h − x₁)/a and (k − y₁)/b are EQUAL — and giving that common value the name r is what makes the rest of the proof short.
steps.memory_tip: m₁m₂ = −1 rearranges to say the two ratios are EQUAL — naming that common value r shortens everything.

recall.must_convey: That m₁m₂ = −1 gives (h − x₁)/a = (k − y₁)/b, and this common value is named r.
accept: perpendicular means m one m two equals minus one, rearrange and call the common value r
the product of the slopes is minus one
h minus x one over a equals k minus y one over b, take it as r
perpendicular kabatti m one into m two equals minus one
name the common ratio r

steps.why: Naming the common ratio r converts two unknowns h and k into ONE unknown, which is the move that makes a two-variable problem solvable in a line.
common_mistakes: Keeping h and k separate and ending with two unknowns and one equation.

steps.label: Write h and k through r
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Read (1) both ways round: each of h and k is now its P-coordinate plus a multiple of r. The point Q is pinned by the single number r.
steps.memory_tip: Each of h and k is its P-coordinate plus a multiple of r, so Q is pinned by one number.
lines: ∴ (h − x₁)/a = r  ⇒  h − x₁ = ar  ⇒  h = x₁ + ar
(k − y₁)/b = r  ⇒  k − y₁ = br  ⇒  k = y₁ + br

recall.must_convey: That h = x₁ + ar and k = y₁ + br.
accept: h is x one plus a r and k is y one plus b r
read the ratio both ways to get h and k in terms of r
express both coordinates through r
h equals x one plus a r, k equals y one plus b r
write h and k using r
heard_as: h equals x one plus a r
k equals y one plus b r

steps.why: With h and k both written through r, any single condition on Q becomes a single equation in r — and that condition is the only place the two proofs differ.
common_mistakes: Writing h = x₁ + br and k = y₁ + ar, with a and b swapped.
Dropping the x₁ or y₁ when rearranging.

steps.label: Find r from the condition
steps.margin_note: The last three marks, and the ONLY place this proof differs from its neighbour. The FOOT of the perpendicular lies ON the line, so its coordinates satisfy the line's equation — substitute and solve for r.
steps.memory_tip: The FOOT lies ON the line, so Q's own coordinates satisfy the equation. Substitute and solve for r.
lines: But Q(h, k) lies on ax + by + c = 0

recall.must_convey: That Q lies on the line, so ah + bk + c = 0, which gives r = −(ax₁+by₁+c)/(a²+b²).
accept: the foot lies on the line so a h plus b k plus c is zero
substitute h and k into the line equation and solve for r
Q is on the line, that is the condition
foot line meeda untundi kabatti a h plus b k plus c equals zero
this gives r equals minus the bracket over a squared plus b squared
heard_as: a h plus b k plus c

steps.why: The foot of a perpendicular is by definition the point where the perpendicular MEETS the line, so it lies on the line — that single fact is the whole of the second half.
common_mistakes: Using the midpoint condition, which belongs to the image proof and gives a factor of 2.
Forgetting to take (a² + b²) common before dividing.
